selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

species_table.rep_name: Economy: full scenario in very few words
Deadpan delivery of an absurd or charged statement
Reliance on a named public figure or current event
Cliche torqued one notch past its ordinary use
Explicit if-then conditional or ultimatum structure
Joke not fully resolved by a self-contained pun
Brevity carrying implied backstory, not brevity as bare label
Sayable as speech, not written-to-be-read prose
Enters mid-conversation, presupposing an unseen prior turn
Institutional or domestic register transplanted intact into an impossible setting
Withholds the gloss; no clause explaining its own joke
Adds an unseen frame rather than annotating what is depicted
Independence from a named topical figure or news-cycle referent
Speaker self-indictment: character exposed rather than scene described
Question whose presupposition is the joke
Dark or morbid content in a mundane frame
Discomfort carried by indirection rather than stated shock
Free of stance markers that instruct the reader to be amused
Deadpan normalization of an extreme or impossible situation
Restraint from numeric or inventory specificity substituting for wit
Direct address of a named individual by first name
Vocative first names and named-addressee direct address
Recycled idiom, catchphrase or borrowed title template
Pre-1990 cultural referents and explicit age self-reference
Named political figures and partisan-aligned targets
Orthographic irregularities from entry form and normalization

selected.name: Natural Spoken Cadence
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds like spontaneous, believable speech with natural rhythm; score 0 when it reads like a slogan, label, or assembled joke fragment.
selected.rationale: R02, R06, R07, and R17 have conversational phrasing, unlike more formulaic lines such as R25 and R49.

selected.name: Verbal Compression
selected.instruction: Score 10 when every phrase efficiently advances the premise or punchline and nothing feels expendable; score 0 when the wording is padded, repetitive, or incomplete.
selected.rationale: R02, R08, R11, and R58 achieve substantial comic implication in very few words.

selected.name: Scene-Conscious Meta-Awareness
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption exploits conventions of conversation, performance, storytelling, or cartoon presentation itself; score 0 when it treats the situation without self-awareness.
selected.rationale: R21, R22, R33, R42, and R60 explicitly play with applause, games, stories, social scenes, or the phrase “in the room.”
member_names: Self-aware or existential meta-commentary by the speaker

selected.name: Revealing Character Voice
selected.instruction: Score 10 when wording distinctly reveals the speaker’s status, attitude, identity, or relationship; score 0 when any anonymous speaker could say it unchanged.
selected.rationale: R14, R17, R37, and R57 communicate strong speaker positions through voice rather than exposition.

selected.name: Concrete absurd escalation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary premise escalates through a specific, disproportionate concrete detail; score 0 when details are random, merely descriptive, or non-escalatory.
selected.rationale: R03 escalates a food order with drywall, and R42 escalates a practical request into an elaborate dishwasher solution.

selected.name: Topical reference integration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a public figure, event, or issue is essential to the joke’s mechanism and is transformed by the wording; score 0 when the reference is detachable name-dropping or a generic opinion.
selected.rationale: R16 turns Trump into bait for bottom feeders, whereas R24 and R38 mainly invoke public figures without developing an equally specific comic mechanism.

selected.name: Late-Line Pivot
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the key reinterpretation or comic reveal arrives at the final phrase after a credible setup; score 0 when the line is flat throughout or reveals its premise immediately.
selected.rationale: R06, R14, R20, R36, and R60 reserve their sharpest change in meaning for the ending.

selected.name: Role/status inversion
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption unexpectedly reverses who has authority, agency, or control; score 0 when relationships remain entirely conventional.
selected.rationale: R34 reveals the speaker as a puppet, while R52 abruptly makes the speaker the listener’s superior.
member_names: Status or power-dynamic reversal between speaker and addressee

selected.name: Visualizable physical staging
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording implies a clear, comic arrangement of bodies, objects, or movement; score 0 when no concrete staging can be inferred from the text.
selected.rationale: R01 supplies a memorable ceiling arrangement, while R48 specifies coordinated action involving a tablecloth and several participants.

selected.name: Deadpan Underreaction
selected.instruction: Score 10 when bizarre or high-stakes circumstances are treated with calm, matter-of-fact language; score 0 when the tone merely matches the event or announces the joke.
selected.rationale: R06, R18, R20, and R60 derive force from understated responses to extreme situations.

selected.name: Freshness beyond stock jokes
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption combines familiar material in an unusually specific angle or formulation; score 0 when it reproduces a predictable pun, cliché, or standard one-liner template.
selected.rationale: R04 and R05 rely on highly familiar wordplay patterns, illustrating how surface cleverness can be mistaken for originality.

selected.name: Implied conversational premise
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds like a natural reply that lets the reader reconstruct an unstated exchange; score 0 when it lacks a believable conversational situation.
selected.rationale: R08 and R52 both imply a power-laden exchange through ordinary dialogue, while their humor depends on what preceded the line.

selected.name: Semantic Hinge
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a word or phrase supports two coherent readings and the line pivots between them; score 0 when wording has only one literal meaning or is merely ambiguous.
selected.rationale: R03, R25, R31, R38, and R49 use words whose alternate meanings create the central turn.

selected.name: Payoff-bearing specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when numbers, objects, names, or technical details materially sharpen the comic premise; score 0 when specificity is decorative, interchangeable, or cluttering.
selected.rationale: R07 uses time and biological details to define the situation, while R45 uses instrument names to make the proposed exchange precise and surprising.

selected.name: Stacked / compound double meanings
selected.instruction: Score whether the caption contains two or more distinct double meanings or puns operating simultaneously, as opposed to a single pun. A 10 has at least two independent, load-bearing wordplay mechanisms both present. A 0 has no wordplay, or exactly one single pun/double meaning.
selected.rationale: R51 ('another job lost to illegal aliens', playing on both immigration anxiety and literal space aliens) and R60 ('stairway to heaven, guys, the short version', stacking a song reference with a literal-stairs meaning) are both card-high/dense-low and both layer more than one simultaneous reading into a short line.

selected.name: Caption length
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of word count, clause count, and elaboration relative to a short one-line caption; judge only textual length, never whether being longer is good.
selected.rationale: R04, R16, R23, and R40 are highly elaborated, while R06, R10, and R50 are very compressed. Length can affect attention and model representation independently of how good the joke is.
member_names: Textual bulk: word count and clause count
upstream_parent_all_members: author's insider knowledge of editorial brevity norms (repeat-entrant savvy)

selected.name: News-cycle / dated-event topicality anchor
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how strongly the caption text ties itself to a specific, datable real-world news event or policy moment (for example a pandemic-era reference to a stimulus payment or mask shortage, or an election-cycle reference) as opposed to describing a timeless, undated scenario. 0 = nothing in the text dates it to a specific news moment; 10 = the caption is unmistakably anchored to one identifiable real-world news event. Do not judge whether the topical reference is clever or well-executed -- score only how strongly the text is anchored to a specific datable event.
selected.rationale: R01 ("full 1200 stimulus") and R15 ("easier to get than an n95 mask") both date themselves to the COVID-relief/pandemic news window and land in dense_low_card_high; if such items were selected partly for topical buzz at submission time rather than caption craft, timeliness is a nuisance, though genuine relatability from shared current events could also make a caption authentically funnier, so it is tagged mixed.
selected.upstream_parent: submission timing relative to news cycle / editorial recency bias
upstream_parent_all_members: submission timing relative to news cycle / editorial recency bias

selected.name: Specific numeric quantity citation
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption includes one or more explicit numbers or counted quantities (a dollar figure, a count of items, a time span given in numerals or number-words) as opposed to using no numbers at all. 0 = no numbers or quantities appear anywhere; 10 = the caption's content is built around one or more explicit numeric quantities. Do not judge whether the specific number chosen is funny or apt -- score only how much explicit numeric quantity is present.
selected.rationale: R01 ("1200 stimulus"), R54 ("four hot dogs, 2 boxes of cracker jack and 2 sheets of drywall"), and R42 ("45 pounds") all foreground explicit numerals and sit in dense_low_card_high; digits stand out visually when many text captions are skimmed together, which is a pure attention artifact unrelated to whether the caption is actually funny.
selected.upstream_parent: numeric-caption visual salience during editorial skim / vote tallying
upstream_parent_all_members: numeric-caption visual salience during editorial skim / vote tallying

selected.name: Vocative first names and named-addressee direct address
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption addresses a specific interlocutor by name or by an explicit relational vocative. 0 = no address term at all; 4 = a generic plural or role vocative ('guys', 'folks', 'ladies and gentlemen', 'sir'); 7 = a personal given name or a kinship vocative ('son', 'honey', 'dad') set off in the utterance; 10 = a named addressee plus a second address term, or a name placed as the caption's rhythmic hinge. Score the presence and prominence of the address term only. Do not judge whether the name is well chosen, whether it adds character or texture, and do not judge the caption's quality.
selected.rationale: Upstream factor: submitters who have read many published captions learn that a dropped-in first name is a house mannerism and insert one to sound published; that is style mimicry, not comic substance. The fingerprint is the vocative: R07 ('we're dinosaurs, ronny'), R57 ('all you want, randy'), R24 ('student of the year is fine, son'), R11 ('stairway to heaven, guys'), R44 ('ladies and gentlemen'). Tagged mixed because a practiced entrant may also genuinely write better, so the parent plausibly causes real quality as well as the mannerism.
member_names: Vocative first names and named-addressee direct address
selected.upstream_parent: veteran-entrant imitation of the venue's published-caption house style
upstream_parent_all_members: veteran-entrant imitation of the venue's published-caption house style

selected.name: Borrowed phrase markers
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of recognizable titles, slogans, idioms, stock lines, or adapted catchphrases; judge only resemblance or allusion, never whether the borrowing is good.
selected.rationale: R16 uses the elephant in the room idiom, R19 references Stairway to Heaven, R49 echoes a familiar troubleshooting line, and R59 uses an applause-sign premise. Template familiarity can prompt recognition without indicating quality, although adaptation can sometimes genuinely help.
selected.upstream_parent: professional assistance or prior exposure to cultural templates
upstream_parent_all_members: professional assistance or prior exposure to cultural templates

selected.name: Conversational scaffolding
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of formulaic dialogue openings or frames such as questions, refusals, guesses, imperatives, or routine replies; judge only presence, never whether the framing is good.
selected.rationale: Routine scaffolds appear in R03, R06, R10, R21, R31, R41, R49, and R50. Such frames may be overrepresented because they resemble common caption templates, creating a text-pattern effect unrelated to entry quality.

selected.name: Ellipsis/dash pause-timing punctuation
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses an ellipsis ("...") or an em/en-dash ("--" or "-") as a mid-sentence pause or delivery-timing marker, as opposed to using only standard sentence punctuation (periods, commas, question marks). 0 = no ellipsis or dash pause marker anywhere in the text; 10 = the caption's structure is built around one or more ellipsis/dash pauses. Do not judge whether the pause improves the caption's timing -- score only how much this punctuation device is present.
selected.rationale: R32 ("...i'll be waiting for a princess... not a prince") and R10 ("it's the trump lure -- it works best with bottom feeders") both use an ellipsis or dash as a formatting habit; this is a pure typographic/layout marker independent of content, though such punctuation is also a recognized craft device for comedic timing, so it is tagged mixed.

selected.name: Scene-anchored concrete object nouns
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption names concrete, physical, picturable objects, settings, or props rather than speaking only in abstractions or pronouns. 0 = no concrete noun at all; the caption is pronouns, generic nouns ('anything', 'it', 'this'), and verbs; 5 = one concrete picturable noun; 8 = two or more concrete picturable nouns; 10 = three or more, or one unusual and highly specific object named as the caption's hinge. Count only the presence and specificity of physical nouns. Do not judge whether the named object fits any drawing, whether the anchoring is skillful, or whether the caption is funny or good.
selected.rationale: A criterion bank almost certainly contains something like 'engages the specifics of the scene', and explicit object nouns are the cheapest way to trip it. The slice splits sharply on this: R08 ('drywall', 'hot dogs', 'cracker jack'), R34 ('chandelier'), R36 ('table cloth'), and R47 ('screen door') carry heavy object vocabulary, while R30 ('did i miss anything'), R59 ('did we forget anything'), R48 ('try not to overthink it') and R16 carry none at all. Tagged mixed because genuine engagement with a drawing can also produce concrete nouns, so the discount must be reported as a sensitivity band rather than applied unconditionally.

selected.name: Specialist abbreviation / acronym shorthand
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses a technical, medical, or otherwise domain-specific abbreviation or acronym (for example a string of periods-separated initials, or specialist shorthand) as opposed to using only everyday plain-language words. 0 = no specialist abbreviation or acronym appears; 10 = the caption's key content depends on a specialist abbreviation or acronym. Do not judge whether the abbreviation is used cleverly -- score only how much specialist shorthand is present.
selected.rationale: R08 ("my husband is an o.b.g.y.n") and R15 ("easier to get than an n95 mask") both hinge on a specialist abbreviation and sit in dense_low_card_high; this is a lexical/orthographic quirk (periods-in-initials formatting, domain jargon) rather than a quality judgment, though an acronym-as-reveal can also be genuine craft, so it is tagged mixed.

selected.name: Editorial elaboration
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption show visibly elaborated syntax, multiple linked clauses, explicit temporal or conditional relations, and carefully maintained referents? Judge only textual elaboration, not writing quality.
selected.rationale: Editing assistance can leave structural fingerprints and can also improve genuine caption quality, making this a sensitivity channel. Elaborated constructions appear in R20, R27, and R55.
